stages.rule: Win 3, draw 1, loss 0; ties by score difference, then head to head.

checkpoint.measure: Score share against fixed practice opponents (0.5 = even)

tiers.label: Practice player = the strongest program (our best)

skills.name: Takes a shot each possession
skills.real: A 3x3 possession has a 12 s shot clock. A team with the ball has to get a shot off; running out the clock is a violation.
skills.measure: Scenario shot (every check ball the program's): the scenario record check balls; Checkpoint Evaluation: the match record fga / own check balls.

skills.name: Makes shots
skills.real: A joint-level shot: release speed, angle and timing come from the program's own joint trajectories; the ring, the ball and the hand are physics.
skills.measure: Scenario shot: field goals made / attempted, seeds pooled; Checkpoint Evaluation: field goals made / attempted.

skills.name: Walks in with the ball before the shot
skills.real: The card's C1 claim: from the 8.5 m check-ball spot a standing shot does not score; the holder walks towards the ring with the ball (walking is dribbling, D19) and then shoots.
skills.measure: Scenario shot: share of the holder's shots released ≥ 1 m closer to the ring than its placement.

skills.name: Keeps a loose ball in view
skills.real: Rebounds, steals and floor balls rely on seeing the ball. The robot has only a head camera: a ball behind it has to be looked for.
skills.measure: Scenario floor: the ball lies still 1.5 m in front of the holder, 20-35 deg off its facing (it starts in its image); over live steps with nobody holding it, the share in which the ball is inside some upright own robot's head-camera frustum. Scenario loose puts it 1.3 m behind-beside (in nobody's image), recorded as the hard search version.

skills.name: Recovers a loose ball
skills.real: A ball on the floor belongs to whoever gets there first: find it, walk to it, squat and pick it up (a joint-level squat takes about 2.9 s) while the opponent goes for it too.
skills.measure: Scenario floor (loose read the same way): share of check balls in which an own robot holds the ball before the opponent and before the 10 s held-ball rule.

skills.name: Stays up after a knock
skills.real: Bumps are routine in a contact game. A robot that stays up keeps playing; a fallen one lies until the next check ball (rule D).
skills.measure: Scenario push: 1.5 s and 5 s after the ball is live each upright own robot gets 0.8 m/s sideways at the pelvis; each robot at each push time is a slot, the share of slots still up 2 s later (a robot already down at the push counts as not up; the scenario record, / k_end). Gate: the same program shoots on every check ball in scenario shot (it plays).

skills.name: Stays up while moving
skills.real: The G1 has no platform gait here; balance is the program's own.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: the match record (upright walking from replay); gate: the team walks ≥ 40 m upright.
skills.line: ≤ 2 falls per robot in 2/3 of matches

skills.name: No gain from contact
skills.real: Pushing and charging are fouls; from the 7th team foul each one gives the other team a point.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: the match record; gate: body contact (≥ 1 s, replay).

skills.name: Acts on time
skills.real: Within a 12 s possession the robot walks, sets and releases; a late step throws the shot off.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation episode cmd rows: share of acts in effect at the step they answer (x1).

skills.name: Walks on its own controller
skills.real: The Engineer seat has no platform gait: walking is the program's own trained or written controller.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: replayed pelvis, upright, from 1.5 s after a placement; scenarios: the scenario record
skills.line: The team walks ≥ 40 m upright a match (16 check balls)

skills.name: Holds the opponent's shooting
skills.real: 3x3 has one basket; the defence stands between the holder and the ring.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: opponent field goals made / attempted (pooled).

off.name: Gets up by itself
off.why: Off the list for now: the reference has no get-up (rule D: a fallen robot lies until the next check ball), so no ablation can move it; in Checkpoint Evaluations almost nobody gets up (reference 1 of 6). Add once a reference gets up.

off.name: Teamwork (passes, screens)
off.why: Excluded on the card: no program passes, nothing to measure.

open_questions: Standing long shot, then a fall. Both models shoot standing from the 8.3-8.5 m check-ball spot (scenario shot: Astra 12/12 made with about 4 acts a check ball; Opus 8/12). The shooter falls after every release. The next check ball re-places every robot, so the fall costs nothing. The card says a standing 8.5 m shot needs >= 11.9 m/s, above the upper-bound thrower probe, yet the models score. Should a fall between the release and the ball's landing be a violation or cost something? Until that is decided, 'Makes shots' has c = partly.

Should 'Walks in with the ball' stay a required skill? The reference shoots by walking in (5/5 shots after >= 1 m) but makes only 1/5 at x1. The standing-shot models read 0 and make more. It could stay as a reading that describes the shot style, without a pass line.

No positive control for seeing and recovering a loose ball. The reference does not go for a floor ball during its own check ball: 0/6 with the ball in front (floor), 0/6 with it behind (loose), and its blind version reads the same, so b cannot move. Astra standing still reads 1.0 in floor, so c fails too. Proposal: read 'Keeps a loose ball in view' only from match play (live ball, nobody holding it: reference 0.40-0.47, Opus 0.26-0.47, Astra 0.02-0.05), and add 'Recovers a loose ball' once a reference does it.

'Stays up after a knock' passes all three checks: reference 39/39, stance-only reference 0/36 (down before the push), do-nothing 0/18. Models: Opus 10/18 at both checkpoints, Astra 0/33 at both (down at every push time, or down at the push). Keep the 2/3 line?

notes.challenge: Three humanoids a side on a half court. The program walks the ball in, stays up in contact and shoots under joint noise, and the check ball starts beyond any standing throw.

achieved.text: Nine matches that were played ended 0:0 and went to a coin toss: two humanoid teams played a whole game and nobody scored.
Shooting separated the field: GPT-6 Astra made 68 of 103 field goals, Claude Opus 5.5 37 of 86, Gemini 4 Argon 8 of 36, Kimi 3.1 Pro 1 of 56.
Kimi's shots kept leaving up to 33 degrees off the line to the hoop through its semifinal, with none made; Astra's eight shots in BSK2-F13 were within 3.2 degrees and seven went in.
In BSK2-F18 Opus shot 0 of 7 with the same release that made 5 of 8 in its previous match; one Astra robot blocked 7 shots.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: Its parameter search started a worker on every CPU core and brought down its own seat.

interface.sees: One head camera per robot (480 × 360, a new frame every 20 ms), each robot's exact position, joints, balance sensors and hands, and the referee's calls. The ball and the other robots appear only in the camera images.
interface.controls: Targets for all 29 joints of each of the three robots, with their own stiffness, and open or close each hand, in real time. Walking, dribbling, passing and shooting are all the agent's own programs.
interface.moment: Final, Claude Opus 5.5 v GPT-6 Astra (0–10), 0:04 in the replay. Astra's robot 1 (red, ringed) gathers the ball beyond the arc, face to face with Opus's robot 1; the long shot that follows scores Astra's first 2 points. Left: what Opus's robot 1 saw.
details: Cameras: one in each robot's head, 480 × 360 pixels, 58° vertical field of view, tilted slightly down. Each camera takes a frame every 20 ms; the newest frame a program can fetch is 40 ms old, stamped with its step.

Own robots: exact position, speed and orientation on the court, the IMU, the 29 joints' angles and speeds as real joint sensors report them (with their noise), torques and targets, the hands, whether a robot holds the ball, and whether it has fallen.

Referee: score, which of the 16 check balls is in play and whose it is, team fouls, game clock and shot clock, possession, whether the ball has been cleared beyond the arc, and every foul with its reason.
Not given: where the ball and the other robots are. The programs find them in the camera images.

Commands, per robot: joint targets for all 29 joints (or only the waist and arms), one row or a sequence of rows 10 ms apart, with optional speeds, extra torque and the stiffness and damping of each joint; a plan of rows for some joint groups; open or close either hand.
How a command moves the robot: targets are held to the joint ranges and speed limits, a PD controller runs at 1 kHz on the noisy joint sensors, and no torque exceeds the motor's limits.
No walking or balance controller: standing, walking, dribbling, passing and shooting are built by the agent. A fallen robot stays down until the next check ball.
Timing: the match runs at real speed and never waits for the agent; a command acts at the next 20 ms step. Commands for several robots sent together act on the same step.
Rules: FIBA 3x3 on a half court; 16 check balls, 8 for each team; a basket from beyond the arc scores 2, from inside 1; more points after the 16th wins.
Before tip-off: 2 hours of preparation with a practice copy of the match world, a practice opponent and a GPU training kit (half an RTX PRO 6000).
